title: Listening in Bairari
hookLine: a tiny raga, a few hymns, easy to hear whole

cards: The Guru Granth Sahib is easy to meet in pieces. One shabad in the morning. A hukamnama, the day's reading opened at random.
A few lines sung in kirtan, then the next raga, the next Guru, the next page. A book this large invites that.

Bairari offers something else: a whole section you can take in at once, start to finish, without losing the thread. A few hymns, a short stretch of pages, and then it's done. Today: listening in Bairari, all of it.

teach.b: It begins where yesterday left off, with Guru Ram Das: sun man, listen, mind, to the untellable story of the Lord's Name. More of his hymns follow, turning the same light around.
One has a refrain worth carrying out of the room. It opens: har jan ram naam gun gaavai.
In paraphrase: the Lord's servant sings the praises of the Name; and if anyone slanders that servant, the servant doesn't lose their own goodness.
Slander is aimed at someone, but here it can't take anything from them. The goodness stays where it was. Then the voice changes.

teach.h: GURU ARJAN: THE SAINTS SING TOGETHER.
teach.b: Guru Arjan, mahala five, closes the section, and his hymn moves from the single listener to a crowd: in paraphrase, the saints met together and sang the Lord's praise, and the pains of countless lifetimes went away.
Hear the whole arc. A mind told to listen. A servant who can't be robbed of goodness by someone else's words.
Alone, then under pressure, then a sangat. Read one hymn and you get a line.
Read all of Bairari and you get a little journey, from listening alone to singing together: the whole of it.

how: Sikhs meet the Granth in daily shabads, in the hukamnama read at random each day, and in kirtan; some also read whole sections or the whole Granth through, and a short raga like Bairari can be read in one sitting.

o: the short raga Bairari, heard whole from start to finish

the first hymn of Bairari, read word by word

games.q: the arc of the raga — tap the pairs.

s: Bairari holds hymns by Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan
Guru Ram Das's hymns, then Guru Arjan's hymn of the saints singing together.
in the refrain, slander strips the servant of goodness
the servant doesn't lose their own goodness, whatever anyone says.

games.q: you sing the praises of the Name, and someone slanders you for it. what does the refrain say you lose?
games.why: har jan ram naam gun gaavai: if anyone slanders the Lord's servant, the servant doesn't lose their own goodness.

practice: If you have a Gurbani app or a printed Granth with meanings, read the Bairari pages straight through, slowly, or play its shabads one after another.
Then sit and hold the shape of it, listening, steadiness, singing together, the way you'd hold a short letter after reading it, without picking a favorite line; if you pray, say Waheguru at the end.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Bairari. The short raga heard whole: a mind told to listen, a servant slander can't rob, and the saints singing together. Today's word.

orig.note: har jan, the Lord's servant, the one Bairari says slander can't rob of goodness.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole of it. Tomorrow, Raga Tilang, where the colors change again. Go gently.
